title: Christians (Acts 11:19–26)
hook: in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tabitha of Joppa, and the coats she made for the widows. Your line was she was full of good works. What did your hands make? Day five hundred forty-five.

For the first years after Jesus, his followers didn't have one name. In Acts they're the disciples, the brethren, the saints, the believers, and people of the Way. Nobody had a word on a sign outside a building. Then, in a big, noisy, mixed city in Syria, somebody gave them a name. The text doesn't say who. And the name stuck so well that today more than two billion people answer to it. It started in a single city, at a single moment, and Luke wrote the moment down.
screen: `DISCIPLES, BRETHREN, THE WAY.` → `NO ONE NAME YET.` → `THEN, ONE CITY.`

segments.voice: The city is Antioch, one of the great cities of the Roman East. After Stephen's death, believers scattered, and most of them shared the message only with fellow Jews. But some men from Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch and spoke to Greeks as well, and a great number believed. Jerusalem hears and sends Barnabas, the son of encouragement. He sees what's happening, and the text says he was glad. Then he does something wise: he goes to Tarsus to find Saul, the new convert from Damascus, and brings him back. The two of them teach in Antioch for a whole year. And then the line, here paraphrased: it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians. In Greek, Christianoi. The ending is a Latin-style one, used for a party or a household: Caesar's people, Herod's people. So the name likely meant Christ's people, the Messiah's crowd. Many scholars think outsiders coined it, maybe half as a joke. The word appears only three times in the whole New Testament: here, from King Agrippa's lips later in Acts, and in First Peter, where believers are told not to be ashamed if they suffer as one. So a name probably given by neighbors became a name people were willing to die for. Antioch has another place in Catholic memory. Tradition says Peter led the church there before Rome. And early in the second century its bishop, Ignatius, wrote the earliest surviving text to call the Church catholic, meaning universal.
screen: `ANTIOCH: JEWS AND GREEKS TOGETHER.` · `BARNABAS FETCHES SAUL.` · `CHRISTIANOI: CHRIST'S PEOPLE.` · `A NICKNAME BECOMES A NAME.` · then, large: `FIRST CALLED CHRISTIANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what the name asks. Settle, and breathe. Whatever name you carry, by faith or family or job, sit with it for a moment. If you are a Christian, notice that the word was first given by neighbors who watched how believers lived. What would your neighbors call you, judging only by this past week? If the name isn't yours, think of a name you do carry, a family name, a team, a title, and what it asks of you. No grading. Just notice. If you pray, you can ask to live up to your name. The bell holds the time.
Christian. Christ's people, the Messiah's people, a name first heard in Antioch and probably given by outsiders. Today's word.
Your line: first called christians. Today, do one thing that would make sense of your name to someone watching. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics receive their Christian name at baptism, often a saint's name, and the Church keeps the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, which once had a separate celebration for Peter's chair at Antioch.

original.note: Greek: Christian, one of Christ's people. Christos means anointed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the name Christians gave themselves.
what it means: in Antioch, where Jews and Greeks believed together, the disciples were first called by a name probably given by others.

what a scholar hears: the -ianos ending is a Latin-style party label, like Herodians. the word occurs only three times in the New Testament, and Ignatius of Antioch is the first known writer to call the Church catholic.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Smyrnaeans 8

notes: Acts 11:26 paraphrased: the Douay-Rheims wording ('first named Christians'?) was not certain enough to quote.
'More than two billion people' is a common estimate of Christians worldwide; confirm.
The -ianus/-ianos ending and outsiders coining the name: widely held scholarly view, not certain; confirm hedging.
Tradition of Peter at Antioch; the separate feast of the Chair of Peter at Antioch (formerly February 22 with Rome on January 18) merged in 1960; confirm the howItsDone wording.
Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 8, earliest surviving use of 'catholic church': standard claim; confirm.
